items.title: Q&A: Mars Perseverance Rover Distance Record
items.summary: On October 11, the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the last five years, Perseverance’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance.Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder Opportunity, which landed on Mars in January of 2004 for a 3-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February of 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity’s entire mission into four minutes, and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15 year life on Mars, doing science as it went: Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers until a planetary-scale dust storm stopped it in its tracks, appropriately enough, in Perseverance Valley.  JPL/YouTube On Feb. 18, 2021, Perseverance joined NASA’s Curiosity rover on the red planet, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter tucked under its belly. Curiosity and Perseverance both ditched Opportunity’s solar panels for a radioisotope thermoelectric generator. Curiosity has been active on Mars since 2012.Despite Curiosity’s nearly 10 year head start, Perseverance is the rover to first break Opportunity’s record. There are several reasons for Perseverance overtaking Opportunity—ruggedized wheels for one—but the biggest contributor is that Perseverance was built for autonomy. To understand how JPL taught a Mars rover to drive itself from 225 million kilometers away without crashing, IEEE Spectrum spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.  This animation shows Perseverance’s point of view during a drive of 807 feet (246 meters) along the rim of Jezero Crater on Dec. 10, 2025, the 1,709th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Captured over two hours and 35 minutes, 53 Navigation Camera (Navcam) image pairs were combined with rover data on orientation, wheel speed, and steering angle, as well as data from Perseverance’s Inertial Measurement Unit, and placed into a 3D virtual environment. The result is this reconstruction with virtual frames inserted about every 4 inches (0.1 meters) of drive progress. JPL-Caltech/NASA Let’s talk about rover autonomy on Mars. Even before Perseverance, rovers were driving themselves, right?Mark Maimone: Yes! Sojourner [in 1997] had an early kind of autonomous behavior—for sensing, it used four laser stripes projected onto the surface, which it used to measure the height of 20 points in the terrain in front of it. It could steer around big obstacles, or even thread the needle between two things. It was a real autonomy system, which is very impressive considering its CPU was less than one megahertz. With Spirit and Opportunity, I developed the autonomy for those rovers. Every time they drove, they would use 256 x 256 pixel stereo pairs to map the geometry of the terrain and find a safe route forward. Spirit actually ended up driving itself 23% of the time, which I was frankly shocked by, since it drove much more slowly in that mode. But using autonomy helped Spirit travel 50% faster than it otherwise could have. Opportunity and Curiosity both only used autonomous driving about 5% of the time. Perseverance is the first Mars rover that drives itself 90% of the time, with its enhanced autonomy system that includes a second processor with an FPGA to do speed up extra image processing operations.What was it like to let Perseverance drive itself for the first time?Maimone: Perseverance is the culmination of decades of work on Mars rover autonomy, so seeing Perseverance use its AutoNav system to drive itself basically at full speed, up to 120 meters an hour, was incredible.  These two images taken by Perseverance’s hazard avoidance and navigation cameras show (on left) the very first AutoNav drive on Mars where the rover autonomously stopped before running into a rock pile, and (on right) the second AutoNav drive where the rover successfully steered around a rock.JPL-Caltech/NASAWhere are the humans in this process?Maimone: The plan of where to go is specified by the science team, and then on the engineering side, the strategic route planning team develops a path to get us to that goal by guessing, based on lower-resolution maps from orbit, what the terrain is going to look like for the rover.
